newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's leading confectioner joins failure list.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's leading confectioner joins failure list.

text.p: The latest South Korean corporate failure is the country's leading confectionery maker, Samlip General Foods Co Ltd, which said on Thursday it would file for court receivership because of heavy debts.
"Our troubles stemmed mainly from payment guarantees on loans taken out by our affiliates," said Kim Jong-ro, assistant manager of Samlip's general affairs division.
"Our companies are not exceptions among those hit by the overall economic slowdown."
Company officials said Samlip had fully guaranteed repayments of 320 billion won ($358 million) borrowed by its five subsidiaries, all unlisted.
"We don't want to ruin our business because of problems with other units," said the company's finance manager.
Real estate developer Samlip Development Co Ltd had been hit hardest by rising financial costs following heavy investments in condominium construction, he said.
The financial status of the mother firm Samlip General Foods worsened after investments to automate its production lines in a new plant outside Seoul, the company's finance manager said.
"We spent about 60 billion won for plant automation," he said.

Samlip General Foods registered losses of 3.5 billion won in 1996 and 11.27 billion in 1995. The company's total debts were estimated at 191.01 billion won at the end of 1996, more than six times its equity capital of 30.52 billion won.
Company officials said Samlip's troubles worsened after the collapse of the nation's second largest steelmaler Hanbo Steel Co in January sent jitters through South Korea's financial system.
"Secondary financial institutions have become very demanding on loan repayments," the finance manager said.
He said Samlip and its affiliates had to repay a total of 50 billion won to secondary institutions in the first four months of the year.
About 60 percent of borrowings by Samlip and its affiliates were from non-banking institutions, he said.
Analysts said secondary lenders have been trying to reduce their exposure to companies deemed to be experiencing financial trouble because their loans were unsecured.
The Korea Stock Exchange suspended trading in Samlip shares indefinitely from Thursday morning. The shares last traded on Tuesday, finishing at 14,300 won. The market was closed on Wednesday.
Traders said the market did not react negatively to Samlip's news. The Korea composite price index soared 2.35 percent on Thursday, mainly on the strength of the yen.
"So many companies are having financial difficulties," said Casey Choe at Union Bank of Switzerland "Investors are becoming less sensitive."
The failure of Hanbo Steel, followed by Sammi Steel Co in March and the near collapse of the Jinro Group set off alarm bells in corporate Korea.
Yu Sung Co Ltd, one of the country's leading makers of woollen textiles, filed for court protection earlier this month because it could not pay its debts.

The Ssangyong, Doosan and Dainong business groups recently announced plans to sell off real estate and merge or sell affilates in an affort to pare costs by focusing on their core business lines. ($1 = 893.10 won)
